question: A previously healthy 2-year-old boy is brought to the clinic with fever and mouth pain that began yesterday. He has consumed an adequate amount of fluids but refuses to eat due to the pain. The patient has no medical problems and takes no medications. Physical examination reveals vesicular, inflamed lesions on the gums and lips. There are no lesions in the posterior oropharynx. He has enlarged and tender cervical lymph nodes. The rest of the examination is unremarkable. Which of the following is most likely responsible for this patient's condition?

options.text: DNA virus, double-stranded, non-enveloped @ Cc DNA virus, single-stranded, non-enveloped

explanation.text: Primary herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) infection is characterized by gingivostomatitis (ie, vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa, particularly the lips and gingivae), fever, and lymphadenopathy. Recurrent HS\V-1 infection (due to viral reactivation) causes lip lesions that are typically less severe due to existing cellular and humoral immunity. HSV-1 and other herpesviruses are enveloped and possess double-stranded DNA genomes. Transmission is usually by direct contact with infected oral secretions or lesions. Inoculation occurs on mucosa or skin where the virus replicates rapidly in the host cell nucleus and causes abnormal cell division, resulting in intranuclear inclusion bodies and multinucleated giant cells visible on Tzanck smear. The vesicular lesions result from cell lysis and necrosis as well as tissue destruction, inflammation, and fluid accumulation between the dermis and epidermis.

(Choice B) Most DNA viruses are double-stranded. They are enveloped (ie, surrounded by a lipid layer) or nonenveloped (ie, lacking a surrounding lipid layer). Adenovirus is a non-enveloped, double-stranded DNA virus that typically causes self-limited upper respiratory infection or gastroenteritis.

(Choice C) Parvovirus is a single-stranded, non-enveloped DNA virus that causes erythema infectiosum, or fifth disease. Patients classically present with fever, cough, and rhinorrhea followed by a "slapped-cheek" and lacy, reticular truncal rash.
(Choice D) Rotavirus, a type of reovirus, is a double-stranded, non-enveloped RNA virus. Rotavirus infection is a vaccine-preventable disease characterized by profuse, watery diarrhea in children.

(Choices E and F) Most RNA viruses are single-stranded and can be classified as negative- or positive-sense viruses. Coxsackievirus, a single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus, causes herpangina, which usually presents with vesicles in the posterior oropharynx, not the anterior oral mucosa. Coxsackievirus also causes hand, foot, and mouth disease, which typically presents with vesicles on the buccal mucosa, tongue, and distal extremities (eg, palms). This patient's anterior mucosal lesions and lack of hand and foot findings are more suggestive of HSV infection.

educational_objective: Primary herpes simplex virus type 1(HSV-1) infection in children causes gingivostomatitis (ie, vesicles on the anterior oral mucosa, particularly the lips and gingivae). HSV-1 and other herpesviruses are double-stranded, enveloped DNA viruses.
